avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

I can no longer trust my own body

issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Checking Behind' and 'Back to Wall' imply a persistent interpersonal pursuit/assault-style danger (someone following me, needing surveillance of the room) that is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Institutional Failure' is not a natural fit with the rest of this MVC profile: the other items center on fragmented accident memory, mistrust of self/body, and hypervigilance, but this appraisal presupposes a salient protector/institution betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type or other selected items.

issues.item: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' does not connect well to the represented triggers, memory, or appraisals. For an MVC case, avoidance is more coherently focused on travel, roads, vehicles, reminders of the crash, or internal trauma cues; avoidance of prior social contacts suggests a different maintaining process that is not otherwise represented.

vignette:
Kofi had spent a lifetime mastering the language of the body. As a dancer, even at sixty-eight, he possessed a grace and physical confidence that belied his age. But that was seven months ago, before the collision. Now, his world had shrunk to the four walls of his apartment, and his body felt like a stranger’s, an unreliable vessel he no longer knew how to command. The accident itself lived in him not as a story but as a collection of sensory shards: the blinding glare of headlights in his rearview mirror, the high-pitched squeal of tires on wet asphalt, and a shattering sound that seemed to come from inside his own head. When he tried to deliberately assemble these pieces into a coherent narrative, they would scatter, leaving him with unnerving gaps and a profound sense of incompleteness.

These gaps in his memory became fertile ground for self-recrimination. He felt that if he couldn't remember the whole event, he couldn't be sure he hadn't done something wrong, some fatal misjudgment in that split second before impact. This uncertainty solidified into a deep-seated conviction that he could no longer trust his own instincts. The fragmented nature of the memory also left him perpetually braced for impact; without a clear beginning, middle, and end, the trauma felt unfinished, capable of recurring at any moment. This feeling was most acute when he heard sudden, loud noises—a car backfiring, a dish dropping—which would instantly transport him back to the terrifying chaos of the crash, his heart pounding in his chest. The memory’s refusal to form a coherent story meant that the threat it contained was never properly filed away as “past.”

His negative beliefs about himself and the world began to dictate his experience of the present. The conviction that his own body was fundamentally unreliable meant that every ache or moment of stiffness, once a familiar part of a dancer’s life, now felt like a harbinger of catastrophic failure. This pervasive sense of physical vulnerability bled into a broader hypervigilance. He also harboured a deep bitterness toward the paramedics who took nearly thirty minutes to arrive, a delay during which he lay trapped and helpless. This experience cemented a belief that the systems meant to protect him were broken, and now, any unexpected delay—a late bus, a slow-moving queue—triggered a surge of anxiety, a feeling that something terrible was unfolding just out of sight. His self-doubt made him hesitant to even try to recall the accident, as if probing the memory would only confirm his own inadequacy in the face of the event.

This triad of a fragmented memory, a constant sense of threat, and corrosive self-doubt drove Kofi into a systematic retreat from the world. Believing he couldn't do the right thing and that his body might fail him at any moment, he began to avoid any situation that felt unpredictable. He stopped going out. The dance studio, once his sanctuary, became a place of imagined peril. He couldn't bear to see the people he used to socialise and rehearse with, certain they would see his fragility. His life, once a fluid performance, became a rigid exercise in risk management. This withdrawal was a direct response to the world feeling like a minefield, a place where his fractured memory offered no reliable map and his own judgment could not be trusted.

The strategies meant to keep him safe, however, only amplified his fear. His apartment, once a place of rest, became a listening post. The more he stayed inside, avoiding the world, the more attuned he became to the sounds from the street, each one amplified and menacing. He arranged his furniture so he could always sit with his back to a wall, his eyes scanning the door. His self-imposed isolation didn't diminish the threat; it concentrated it, confirming his belief that danger was everywhere, just waiting for him to let his guard down. By avoiding old friends, he lost the very connections that might have reassured him, leaving him alone with his terrifying thoughts.

It was the profound loneliness that finally brought Kofi to therapy. His life had become a waiting game, a small, quiet existence devoid of the movement, music, and community that had once defined him. He came to his first session not with a clear hope for recovery, but with a desperate, whispered question: was there any way to trust his own body, and the world, again?
